title: Can We Detect Failures Without Failure Data? Uncertainty-Aware Runtime Failure Detection for Imitation Learning Policies
methods: one-class failure scores learned from successful rollouts only (flow-based density logpZO, RND)
question: Can failures of generative imitation-learning policies be detected at runtime using only successful data, with statistical control of false alarms?
key_findings: Inputs to the score are the policy's own jointly trained visual features plus robot state and generated future actions; failures are treated as out-of-distribution relative to successful rollouts.
Average best balanced accuracy across score candidates is about 78% in simulation and about 72% on robot hardware.
Learned scores beat post-hoc ones: logpZO is top-1 in 10 of 16 simulation cases and 8 of 12 hardware scenarios.
STAC's detection time exceeds the average successful trajectory time, so it detects failures too late to be useful.

evidence.scale: about 2000 rollouts per simulation task, 50 rollouts per hardware task
evidence.statistics: partial: conformal guarantees on false-positive rate; accuracies reported as point values per setting
evidence.baselines: STAC, PCA-kmeans, SPARC and other post-hoc scores

causal_validation: No: detection only, no intervention on the features used.
closed_loop: Detection runs online during closed-loop execution; no intervention.
critique: Not a VLA paper, but it is the most cited failure-detection precedent inside the VLA monitoring literature (cited by 7 of the downloaded papers) and sets the one-class, conformal framing that SAFE and its successors adopt or argue against.
Balanced accuracy around 72-78% leaves many missed failures or false alarms; the guarantee is on false positives, not on catching failures early.
code: project website linked in the paper
one_line: Failure detection for diffusion and flow robot policies trained only on successful rollouts, using the policy's own features and actions with conformal thresholds; about 78% balanced accuracy in simulation and 72% on hardware.
